items.title: A tree that died yesterday is 'older' than one from 1955
items.claim: Radiocarbon dating assumes atmospheric carbon-14 is roughly constant. Nuclear weapons testing in the 1950s and 60s doubled atmospheric C-14. Trees that grew then have unusually high C-14, and a sample that died yesterday now looks older than one from 1963.
items.prompt: What is the modern correction for this 'bomb spike'?

options.text: Radiocarbon dating no longer works for anything after 1945
Calibration curves use tree rings and other archives to map measured C-14 to true age — the bomb spike actually makes recent dating MORE precise
Scientists subtract a fixed amount from all measurements after 1945
All organic material dated after 1945 is considered modern and unmeasurable

items.reveal_title: Calibration turns a bug into a feature
items.reveal:
Dendrochronology (tree ring sequences) extends back over 13,000 years and gives a year-by-year record of atmospheric C-14. The 1955 to 1963 'bomb spike' nearly doubled C-14 concentrations, then decayed away as CO2 mixed into oceans.

Forensic scientists now use this spike to date tissues with about 1-year resolution: bone, hair, even individual lenses of the eye. It turned out that lens fibre cells preserve a chemical timestamp of the year they formed. Atmospheric pollution became a precision dating tool.
items.why: Constants are assumed to be constant. Real-world calibration is more subtle and often more interesting than the textbook formula.

items.title: Pure water dissolves more silver chloride than salt water does
items.claim: Silver chloride is famously insoluble — Ksp is about 1.8 times 10 to the minus 10. But it dissolves slightly. Try to dissolve it in salt water and the solubility plummets to almost zero.
items.prompt: Why does adding more Cl- decrease AgCl solubility?

options.text: Le Chatelier — adding more Cl- shifts AgCl(s) is in equilibrium with Ag+ + Cl- back to the left, reducing dissolved Ag+ until [Ag+][Cl-] equals Ksp again
Silver chloride decomposes in salt water
Salt water becomes saturated with itself, leaving no room for AgCl

items.reveal:
Suppose in pure water solubility 's' equals square root of Ksp, around 1.3 times 10 to the minus 5 M for AgCl.

In 0.1 M NaCl, [Cl-] is dominated by the salt (about 0.1 M). [Ag+] must satisfy [Ag+] times 0.1 equals 1.8 times 10 to the minus 10, so [Ag+] is about 1.8 times 10 to the minus 9 M. Solubility drops by a factor of nearly 10,000.

This is exploited in gravimetric analysis: precipitate the analyte by adding excess of a common ion, ensuring almost everything comes out of solution.
items.why: Students think 'dissolved + dissolved = more dissolved'. Le Chatelier flips the intuition for ionic equilibria.

items.title: Certain numbers of protons and neutrons make nuclei extra stable
items.claim: Helium-4, oxygen-16, calcium-40 and lead-208 are all unusually abundant and stable. They have 'magic numbers' of protons and/or neutrons: 2, 8, 20, 28, 50, 82, 126.

options.text: Nuclei have a shell structure analogous to electron shells — completed proton or neutron shells confer extra binding energy and stability; this is the nuclear shell model
These numbers correspond to particle masses
They are leftover from the Big Bang

items.reveal:
Maria Goeppert-Mayer and J. Hans D. Jensen (1949) proposed that nucleons in a nucleus, like electrons in an atom, occupy quantum shells. Closed shells (magic numbers: 2, 8, 20, 28, 50, 82, 126) give exceptional binding energy.

Lead-208 is doubly magic (82 protons, 126 neutrons) — it is the heaviest stable nuclide. Oxygen-16 (8 and 8) and calcium-40 (20 and 20) are also doubly magic.

The search for an 'island of stability' near a hypothetical doubly magic superheavy nucleus (around Z=114, N=184) drives much modern heavy-element research. Goeppert-Mayer and Jensen shared the 1963 Nobel Prize.
items.why: Nuclear physics seems disconnected from quantum mechanics. The shell model says nuclei obey the same quantum-mechanical patterns as atoms — at a wildly different energy scale.
